Yes. The students make an H1 of a standard object, the one above, on the first day. This makes life easy for us because we know the best lighting and can set it up quickly. On the second day, they shoot a reflection, image planed H2 fromf the H1 of the previous day. We all set up the reflection H2, they decide on the image plane (so thay can get a "feel" for the way a plane goes through the 3D volume of the image) and I shoot the first one. After that, they all take it turns to shoot one each. The one above is the first piece I shot for the last class.

You may be right about the bandwidth, but every time I bring up the photopic curve, I get no reply. What is the effect of increased bandwidth on a hologram? If the bandwidth were from, say 350-450 there's a 100nm bandwidth. Also a 100 nm bandwidth from 530-630. Which is "brighter"?

My point was that PFG-01 can make very bright holos. I was answering a point made that PFG-01 "may not" be as bright as PFG-03. There was no question as to the geometry of the shot. I thought that the caveat abiout the word "may" was pretty deceptive. Clearly the writer did believe that 01 could not make as bright a holo as 03 based purely on the published resolution of the two films on the Slavich site. In this case, I was referring to the properties of the emulsion as a function of the brightness and this is independant of the geometry of the shot. I could just as easily have made a Denisyuk and stolen some light to re-illuminate around the plate and so increase the ratio, so I don't think the fact that it's not a denisyuk takes away from my argument that 01 can make pretty bright holos and it has nothing to do with the resolution. If anyone can make a similar comparison between 03 and DCG, I'd be happy to look at it. I have not yet seen a 03 hologram as bright as this. Also, I have yet to see a paper connecting the "brightness" of a hologram with the spatial frequency response of the emulsion, as the writer seemed to indicate when he said "..01 may not be as bright". I thought this connection was tenuous at best and completely unsupported by any data. Kogelnik deals a little with this but only for a uniform grating with constant frequency. there is nothing in Kogelnik about bandwidth. I know some will disagree, so perhaps they can point out the exact equation in the Kogelnik paper dealing with either the "brightness' vs spatial frequency, or "brightness" at all.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: You're right. You did say, "high quality" not "bright". In that sense, I misread it. 03 does have a "higher quality" insofar as clarity is concerned. The problem is that holographic parameters are so notoriously subjective that I'm afraid everytime I hear, "it's bright" or even "...incredibly bright" I wonder what's actually meant. Most pics of holograms have nothing else in the picture, sometimes not even the edges of the film/glass. So what's "bright" being compared to - a white wall in direct sunlight? The actual object under the same illumination as the hologram? I feel that holographers tend to see display (or pictorial as Bob says - I'm beginning to like the word!) holograms as a "technical" thing because of it's roots and associations - Gabor, Leith/Upatniks, Kogelnik etc whereas they're really not. They're objects being illuminated. True the object is being created by a diffractive ("technical") process, but the image of the hologram is no different than the image of an object projected by a curved mirror a la the Disney ghosts. In that sense, words like "effficency", "bright" or even "colour" don't have the same "force" as "clarity", "sharpness", "hue" etc. I suppose I've become oversensitive to The Names misuse of terms and limited understanding of the subject. Because they're Names, their views are always "correct" and someone who's not a Name gets ignored. So "zero order tables" is an accepted name because a Name (I won't say who) doesn't understand that "zero order" referes to a mathematical term in the diffractive series - not a table geometry. Or that you 'have to' shoot at "Brewster's angle" (whatever that is) otherwise you won't get a hologram. Or that a ttransmission hologram is "thin" and a reflection hologram is "thick" and that one is seen with reflected light and the other with transmitted light.
